name: Skillscope — see what a skill actually tells your agent to do
one_liner: For anyone about to run `npx skills add <repo>`, Skillscope takes the repo or a pasted SKILL.md and returns a one-screen X-ray: what the skill tells your agent to do in plain English, every file/network/shell capability it requests, and the suspicious lines highlighted.
problem: Agent skills are now installed with a single command (`npx skills add jakubkrehel/skills`, ClawHub, skills.sh, VS Code, Gemini CLI). A skill is markdown plus optional scripts that your agent reads and obeys — but nobody reads the markdown. Today people either install blind off an X post, or run a security CLI (Snyk mcp-scan, NVIDIA SkillSpector, ClawVet) that prints a CVE-style verdict for security engineers. Neither answers the question a curious developer actually has in the 15 seconds before installing: "what will this thing make my agent do, and does it touch my files, my shell or the network?" Skillscope is that: paste a repo URL or drop a SKILL.md, get a readable capability card with the risky lines quoted inline, shareable as a link.
target_customer: Developers installing agent skills/plugins for Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot and OpenClaw — the crowd that reposted the /teardown skill. They hang out on X (AI dev side), r/ClaudeAI, r/codex, Hacker News, and awesome-agent-skills lists. Skill authors are the second audience: they will paste their own repo to get a badge showing their skill is clean.
why_now: Skills became one-command installs across Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, VS Code and OpenClaw in 2026, and this year's scans (Snyk: 36.8% of 3,984 skills with a flaw, 13.4% critical; NVIDIA SkillSpector: 26.1% of a 31k subset) made the risk concrete — while every existing tool is a CLI for security engineers, not a link you can send.
comparables: Snyk mcp-scan (https://snyk.io/blog/toxicskills-malicious-ai-agent-skills-clawhub/) — free CLI, security-grade findings, terminal-only, audience is AppSec, no shareable output. NVIDIA SkillSpector (https://github.com/nvidia/skillspector) — open-source scanner, static + semantic checks, again a CLI with a report file. ClawVet — MIT scanner for OpenClaw SKILL.md files, same shape. Skill directories (localskills.sh, skills.sh, awesome-agent-skills) list and rank skills but show you a README, not what the skill instructs. Backslash Security writes about enterprise skill approval workflows (https://www.backslash.security/learning/how-to-approve-ai-skills-without-slowing-developers-down) — a paid governance angle, not a public one-click reader. Gap: nothing is a no-install web page where you paste a repo, see a plain-English "this skill will…" summary plus a capability badge row, and send the link to a teammate.
risks: Prior art is real and respected: if Snyk or NVIDIA ships a hosted web UI, the wedge thins fast — so the differentiator must stay "readable and shareable", not "more accurate". Second, a false red badge on a popular author's skill is a reputational landmine; the card has to quote the exact line and never render a grade. Third, one-time curiosity: most people x-ray one repo, share it, and never return unless the gallery and a CI/badge hook give them a reason.
validation_test: Ship the static gallery version Saturday with 30 pre-scanned popular skill repos and post the X draft with a 20-second screen recording of the auto-poster card (red badges + the piped-curl line quoted). Pass if ≥300 people paste their own repo in the first 48 hours, or if any skill-directory or scanner maintainer (localskills.sh, SkillSpector, awesome-agent-skills) links to it. Fail if people only look at the gallery and nobody submits a repo — that means it reads as a blog post, not a tool.
build_plan: Stack: Next.js + Tailwind on Vercel, TypeScript (builder's language), no database for v1. Steps: (1) Fetch route takes a GitHub repo URL or org/repo shorthand, pulls SKILL.md files and any scripts via the public GitHub API — no auth needed for public repos. (2) Deterministic pass in plain TS: regex/AST-lite detection of capability signals — curl/wget, shell-out, `rm`, env var and credential reads, base64 blobs, outbound URLs, file writes outside the workspace, "ignore previous instructions"-style injection phrases. These are cheap and are what make the card trustworthy. (3) One model call (any long-context cheap model) with a strict JSON schema: `what_it_does` (3 bullets), `agent_will` (imperative list), `watch_out` (quoted line + why). (4) Render a card: title, capability badges (Files / Shell / Network / Secrets / Installs code), the three sections, and every flagged line quoted with a jump link to the file on GitHub. (5) Shareable permalink `/s/owner/repo` with OG image generation so the card previews in an X post, plus a copy-as-markdown button. (6) Pre-scan ~30 popular public skill repos so the homepage is a browsable gallery, not an empty box. Cut for v1: accounts, CI integration, private repos, scoring/grading numbers, any claim of being a security product (label it "a reader, not an audit"), MCP servers.
launch_post:
You install agent skills with one command. Have you read one?

Paste any skill repo into Skillscope and get a one-screen X-ray: what it tells your agent to do, what it touches (files, shell, network, secrets), and the sketchy lines quoted.

Free, open source, no install.
reasoning: Skillscope beat the others on the build track because it sits exactly where the builder's taste lives — one input box, a result in seconds, no signup, open source, and the result itself is the shareable artifact (like Napkins' before/after) — while riding something genuinely new: skills-as-one-command-installs plus 2026's scan data. It is a weekend of TypeScript and a GitHub API call for someone who already works with agents daily, and the deterministic regex layer means it is useful even if the model call is cheap and shallow. The failure mode I can route around is one-time curiosity: pre-scanning 30 popular repos turns it into a browsable gallery people revisit, which is the 1kpapers move from the bookmarks. could_grow is true: the same card is the thing a platform team needs before approving a skill internally, which is the paid version (Backslash is already selling that story to enterprises). Pain is expressed — Snyk, NVIDIA, Orca and CSA all published on it this year and developers complain about installing skills blind. Nothing here repeats the library: Driftwatch watches vendor changelogs for an integration owner and Holdroom supervises live phone agents; Skillscope reads an artifact before install for a public developer audience. The runner-up venture, Dossier, is a different buyer (the founder mid-raise) and a different workflow (answering diligence requests) from anything filed, but it loses on gap — Papermark, Peony and Ideals all ship AI document Q&A in the room already, so it is a watch, not a dig.
candidates_considered:
1. Skillscope (build) — WON. Paste a skill repo, get a plain-English capability X-ray. Fresh, shareable, a weekend.
2. Manualess, photo/PDF → illustrated step guide (build), from nutlope's IKEA post — dropped: the inspiring post IS this, and building it is a thin clone; BILT (bilt.ai) owns the commercial side and the hard part is generating accurate part illustrations, which is weeks not a weekend.
3. Teardown-as-a-web-app, upload object photo → annotated exploded SVG (build) — dropped: direct clone of @jakubkrehel's /teardown, and Layer already ships a hosted Technical Diagram Generator (layer.ai/tools/layer--technical-diagram-generator).
4. Dossier (venture) — diligence request list → drafted, cited answers for founders mid-raise. Survived research but gap is closing: Papermark (€99-149/mo), Peony ($30 tier with AI document Q&A), Ideals all do in-room AI Q&A. Kept as runner_up at 6.4.
5. Mia-for-B2B, AI short-form sales video agent (venture) — dropped: crowded, undifferentiated vs every UGC-ad generator, no clear owner with budget, and search surfaced multiple "AI salesperson" startups already.
6. Vocal-shortcut pack for agent voice triggers (build), from the "Hey Grok" post — dropped: it is a settings tutorial, not software; nothing to ship and nothing to open source.
research_notes: 10 tool calls. Web Summary on the skills ecosystem confirmed `npx skills add` installs third-party SKILL.md packages that agents read and obey — which turned the /teardown bookmark from "nice illustration demo" into "people install arbitrary agent instructions in one command". Web Summary on Papermark gave real pricing (€99/mo annual, €149 monthly, tiers to €999) and named competitors, which sized the runner-up and showed in-room AI Q&A is already shipping. Searches for IKEA-manual AI tools surfaced BILT (bilt.ai) and the AssemblyLens paper, killing candidate 2; a search for technical-illustration generators surfaced Layer's hosted Technical Diagram Generator, killing candidate 3. The decisive search was on agent-skill supply-chain security: Snyk's ToxicSkills (3,984 skills scanned, 36.8% flawed, 13.4% critical), NVIDIA SkillSpector (26.1% of 31k subset), ClawVet, and the CSA research note — all CLIs and reports, none a shareable web reader. A follow-up search for skill directories (localskills.sh, awesome-agent-skills, skills.sh) and for enterprise skill-approval products (Backslash, Speakeasy MCP Gateway) confirmed the listing and governance ends are taken but the public one-click reader is open, and suggested the venture path for could_grow. I could not view any of the videos in these bookmarks and did not guess at their contents.
prototype_summary: Skillscope prototype: paste a skill repo name, watch a simulated SKILL.md read, and get an X-ray card showing capability badges, what the skill does, imperative "your agent will…" lines, and expandable flagged source lines across five hard-coded demo repos.
